codes.consistency_notes: 2008: summing R5777 Table 3 sports-betting Ns (110+7+419+72 = 608; 79 at-risk) gives 13.0% at PGSI 3+. R2661 Table 5 reports 13.1%. These counts are weighted (R5777: 'After weighting, the number of included respondents was 8917'). The Table 2 percentages × group Ns agree with the Table 3 Ns (9.9% × 4227 ≈ 419; 25.4% × 285 ≈ 72; 2.6% × 4228 ≈ 110; 3.9% × 179 ≈ 7). R5777 has internal discrepancies: the text says 463 at-risk (284 males), but Table 2 gives 285 male AR, and the Table 2 Ns sum to 8,919 rather than 8,917. The 2008 sports question included event betting. 2014: the R2661 Methods say SGHV 2014 was not used for frequency analysis, yet Tables 1, 4 and 5 report 2014 monthly and weekly sports-betting estimates. R2661 gives no counts for sports bettors in any year, so its estimates are weighted percentages only (cases and n = NR). The 2014 and 2018 response rates are frame-specific, so response_rate is NR and the rates are quoted.
codes.note: I extracted three samples (2008, 2014, 2018). The 2008 and 2014 surveys used the Queensland 5-point modified PGSI response scale, which R5777 calls non-validated; 2018 used the original PGSI. Only 2008 has traceable counts, and those are weighted counts from R5777 (n = 608; at-risk 79). For 2014 and 2018, the sports-bettor n can only be approximated from weighted participation (~650 and ~617). R2661 states no funding source in the text provided.

codes.consistency_notes: Participant flow: 24,829 invited, 3,867 accessed, 1,959 completed up to the PGSI, 1,647 completed all PGSI items (the analysed sample), 1,470 answered every question, and 1,580 completed the GHM. Table 1 counts PGSI harm as 448 + 406 = 854 and no harm as 24 + 702 = 726, which add to 1,580. These are the GHM completers, which is why the table shows 854 rather than the 893 PGSI-harmed reported among all 1,647. Table 3 note: 592 people did not report income, leaving 1,055 (1,647 - 592 = 1,055, which matches). For the 18-25 subgroup, 87 GHM-harmed is printed as 41%. That does not fit a denominator of 239 (it would be 36.4%), so the GHM denominator for this group is unreported. The Discussion says GHM harm affected 'just under 30% of the unweighted sample' (472/1,580 = 29.9%) and PGSI harm 'slightly more than half' (893/1,647 = 54.2%). Both agree with the counts.
codes.note: One sample: online wagering customers of one operator (Entain) in Australia. The sample mixes sports and race betting, and no sports-only estimate is reported. The study does not report standard PGSI categories (0, 1-2, 3-7, 8+). Problem gambling is reported only as a modified 7-item PGSI harm index (items scored 0/1, harmed at 2 or more) and as GHM harm. Both are coded not_levelled, so for prevalence purposes this study fits only the ad hoc / evidence-map strand.

codes.excluded_samples: Not extracted: the whole-sample prevalence estimates in Table 2 (sample 1 n=3,795; sample 2 n=5,514, by sex), because they cover all pupils, not sports bettors. Also not extracted: offline sports bettors (and online and offline combined), because they appear only as regression predictors in Table 3 (merged active gamblers, N=3,663) with no prevalence. The paper has no treatment, helpline or self-exclusion samples.
codes.consistency_notes: 1) Discussion gives 2.2% (sample 1) and 1.7% (sample 2) for problematic gambling among all pupils. This matches Table 2: (68+14)/3,795 = 2.16% and (77+14)/5,514 = 1.65%. 2) Discussion says that among past-year gamblers the rate is 4.9% in sample 1 and 3.8% in sample 2. Table 1 gives sample 1 active gamblers as 997+562 = 1,559, and 82/1,559 = 5.3%, not 4.9%. Sample 2: 91/(1,495+866) = 3.85%, which matches. 3) Table 1 for sample 2 has apparent typos: '196 (127)' (probably 19.6) and '630 (28.6)' (values swapped). 4) pct_male is computed from Table 2 for the whole school sample (sample 1: 1,843/3,795 = 48.6%; sample 2: 2,757/5,514 = 50.0%). It does not describe the sports bettors. 5) Age range 12-18 is for the whole school sample; mean age is reported only by gambling-status group (Table 1), not for the sample overall or for sports bettors. Age group is coded mixed because 18-year-olds are included.
codes.note: Two separately recruited state school surveys, so two samples. The only sports-betting estimate is the percentage with problematic gambling among past-year online sports bettors (DSM-IV-MR-J >=4): 20.2% in sample 1 and 19.8% in sample 2. No counts or denominators are given, so cases and n are NR. Mode of administration (paper vs electronic) is not stated; it is probably a paper questionnaire in class. Legal status is coded NR: the text only says gambling is prohibited for minors in Germany and that Internet gambling is 'almost completely unregulated'. instrument_validated_in_language = yes rests on the authors' general statement 'a validated self-report measure'. The German version is cited to Hurrelmann et al. 2003, which is not explicitly a validation study, so the reviewer should check this (it also affects JBI 6).

(2) R3634 Table 1 at T0 gives PGSI 3+ = 507, but the R4056 sex tables add up to 508 (289+59+135+25). PGSI 0 (2,670) and PGSI 1-2 (688) match exactly. (3) R3634 calls the T0 data the pre-pandemic period. The wave-1 PGSI, however, refers to the 3-month lockdown (mid-March to mid-June 2020), as R4056 and R3634 both state. (4) R4056 gives weighted percentages with unweighted counts; R3634 does not use weights. (5) There are small errors in R4056 Table 3a: the age band percentages (35.5% is printed twice) and conflict 'About the same 2087 (14.9%)'. Neither affects the PGSI counts. (6) In R3634 the T0 mean spend for PGSI 3+ is £1050.10 in the text but £1010.50 in Table 1; this is not relevant to prevalence.
codes.note: The whole-sample PGSI estimates were derived by adding the male and female counts in R4056 Tables 2a/2b. R4056 gives weighted percentages only by sex. Sampling was coded quota (non-probability YouGov panel); there is no explicit quota design.

samples.notes: Sample = respondents reporting past-12-month online sports betting (incl. fantasy sports) among 83 past-year online gamblers in a national survey of 2000 adults. The separate category 'online betting on e-sports or online virtual sports' (n=11) is extracted as a subgroup. Its overlap with the 19 sports bettors is not reported, so the union cannot be computed. Age and sex fields describe the whole sample of 2000; they are not reported for sports bettors. Offline gambling was not measured, so land-based sports bettors are not captured. Interviewers could substitute a person of the same age and sex if the drawn respondent was unavailable. The Polish BBGS was validated in adolescents and was reworded for online gambling in this study (an unvalidated modification). Data were collected in December 2018, the same month new online games were introduced.

codes.consistency_notes: Text: 22 of 83 online gamblers at risk, reported as "26.8%". 22/83 = 26.5%. Table 4 NPeG percentages for sports betting (11 = 18.3%) and esports (10 = 16.7%) imply a denominator of 60, not 61. The gender column for NPeG also sums to 60 (45+15), so some NPeG items appear to have one missing answer. In Table 4, sports betting counts (11+8=19) and esports counts (10+1=11) match the Table 2 totals of 19 and 11. Table 1 lists children "Yes 268 (63.4%)" and "No 732 (36.6%)". These numbers do not add up, and 268 looks like a typo for 1268.
codes.note: This draft was built from the reverse-table rule using Table 4 (problem vs non-problem online gamblers by game type). Very small n (19 sports bettors). The brief BBGS screen was reworded for online gambling.
